preamble: Cass often goes up to her grandad's allotment with him at weekends. On this Saturday they have come to dig the potatoes.
body:
We went up to the allotment on the Saturday because the potatoes were ready and Grandad said he was not going to let them go back to sleep in the ground.

It is a fifteen-minute walk from his flat. We did it in about thirty-five, because he stopped at the bottom gate to look at Denise's dahlias and then again halfway up the path to look at nothing in particular, holding the water butt with one hand and taking his breath the careful way you carry a glass you have filled too full.

"Staked late," he said. "She does it every year and every year they go over in the wind." Denise's dahlias were taller than me and him put together, but I did not say so, because it was not that kind of conversation.

The shed key lives on his belt loop. He put his hand down for it and it was not there, and he said that of course it wasn't, he had moved it for Alan, it would be under the brick. It was under the brick. So that was that.

Inside the greenhouse the tomato leaves had curled in on themselves and gone crisp, like paper that has been left near a fire. Grandad said he had given them a proper soak on Tuesday and it was the sun coming through the glass that finished them, this weather, unbelievable. The water butt outside was full to the lid. I said the weather had been unbelievable, which it had.

Then he showed me the potatoes. You put the fork in a hand's width back from the stem so you do not spear them, and if you hear a noise like a knife going into an apple you have done it wrong and should stop pretending you have not. He did the first root. Then he sat down on the upturned crate and supervised, and supervising mostly meant telling me the fork was too close. They came up pale, with the earth dropping off them in lumps, and he counted them into the bucket out loud and lost his place twice and started again from where he thought he had got to.

Alan from plot fourteen came over with a marrow he did not want and stood at the end of the row.

"All right, Ted. All right, Cass. I'll get the beans in Thursday."

"If I'm about," Grandad said.

"You'll be about," Alan said, and went off down the path.

Grandad told me that Alan was taking the plot on from the autumn, only until the knee was sorted out, and that Alan could not grow a leek to save his own life but he turned up, which counts for more. Then he said that when the garlic went in in November he would want me up here to do the string for him, because his knots had gone useless and mine were neat. I said I would come. I like doing the string.

We had the sandwiches on the crate at one o'clock, because he eats at one. He got through half of his and passed me the rest and said he had had an enormous breakfast. He does have enormous breakfasts. He always has.

He said Mum was driving him somewhere on Thursday and it was nothing, they just like to be thorough these days, and that the parking there costs a fortune, three pounds twenty for the first hour. I said that was a scandal. He said it was exactly that.

He would not let me take both buckets, so he had one handle and I had the other and we went down the path sideways like a crab.

When we locked up he did not put the key back under the brick. He put it into my hand and closed my fingers over it the way he does with a pound coin, and said I might as well hang on to it, it would save him hunting about every time. Then he leaned his shoulder on the shed door to get it shut and pulled twice at the padlock to be sure of it.

"Don't let me forget the garlic," he said.
